A0025.title: Digital Certificate
A0025.definition: Digitally signing and encrypting data or files through a digital certificate mechanism.
A0025.description: Unlike API signature verification (A0002), digital certificates place more emphasis on the integrity of the entire transmission chain from sender to receiver, and can also serve as a mechanism for verifying the sender's authenticity. API signatures focus more on ensuring the integrity of data passed from the client and across sites. Simply put, digital certificates primarily protect the data transmission process, while API signatures primarily protect the user terminal.
A0025.limitation: Since digital certificates are issued by trusted third-party authorities, the security of digital certificates is heavily dependent on the trustworthiness of the issuing authority. If the issuing authority is compromised, attackers can forge digital certificates. Additionally, the security of digital certificates is also affected by the signing algorithm — if the signing algorithm is compromised, attackers can forge digital signatures.

A0025-001.title: Email Digital Certificate
A0025-001.definition: Providing trustworthiness guarantees for email senders and integrity and confidentiality guarantees for email content.
A0025-001.description: Digitally signing and encrypting emails and attachments provides a high level of confidentiality and security for electronic communications. Encryption means only the intended recipient can read the email, while digital signatures allow them to confirm the sender and verify that the email was not tampered with in transit. (Excerpted from Tencent Cloud)
A0025-001.limitation: Using email digital certificates can be relatively complex — users need to understand the concept of digital certificates, purchase certificates, configure email clients, etc. This may create a barrier for general users. Digital certificates need to be renewed on time, and updates must be performed before expiration. Certificate management can become complex, especially for large-scale deployments. For end-to-end encryption and signing to work, both the sender and recipient must support and configure digital certificates, which may impose limitations when communicating with users who do not use digital certificates. Email digital certificates can only provide security during transmission and cannot address endpoint security issues such as password leaks or malware infections.

A0025-002.title: HTTPS Digital Certificate
A0025-002.definition: Providing trustworthiness, integrity, and confidentiality guarantees for HTTP requests.
A0025-002.description: By purchasing and installing an HTTPS certificate service, the server identity is authenticated, and the transmission of HTTP requests is protected with integrity and confidentiality guarantees to prevent man-in-the-middle tampering and eavesdropping.
A0025-002.limitation: The security of HTTPS digital certificates heavily depends on the trustworthiness of the issuing authority. If the issuing authority is compromised, an attacker can forge digital certificates, thereby undermining the security of HTTPS digital certificates. Additionally, the security of HTTPS digital certificates is also affected by the signature algorithm. If the signature algorithm is compromised, an attacker can forge digital signatures, thereby undermining the security of HTTPS digital certificates.

references.title: Transport Layer Security Cheat Sheet - OWASP

A0025-003.title: Electronic File Seal
A0025-003.definition: Applying electronic seals to electronic contracts, orders, and agreements based on PKI digital certificates, using digital signatures and timestamps to guarantee signer authenticity and document integrity.
A0025-003.description:
An electronic file seal uses the signer's digital-certificate private key to sign the document digest, binding the signature value, certificate, and timestamp to the file to form an independently verifiable seal. Any tampering with the document or seal causes signature verification to fail, providing authenticity, integrity, and non-repudiation for online contracting scenarios such as electronic contracts, orders, and agreements.

Unlike digital certificates (A0025), which focus on transport-link trust, electronic file seals target the document entity itself across its full lifecycle: a trusted timestamp fixes the signing sequence at signing time, and preservation services anchor the seal and document hash on-chain or with a third-party evidence platform, so that disputes can yield electronic evidence admissible under electronic-signature law. It is commonly combined with file-preservation and contract-management platforms to cover online contracting, historical-contract tracing, template management, and real-time evidence collection.
A0025-003.limitation: The trustworthiness of an electronic seal depends entirely on the underlying PKI and CA: if a CA is breached and issues forged certificates, or a private key is stolen via terminal malware or a lost USB Key, attackers can impersonate the subject to affix legitimate seals. Verification also relies on trusted timestamp and preservation services; in offline or cross-platform scenarios users often cannot recognize forged files because they are unfamiliar with seal verification, leaving a high usage barrier for general users.

references.title: Recommendation for Key Management - NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5

A0025-004.title: USB Key Digital Certificate
A0025-004.definition: A USB interface hardware device with a built-in microcontroller or smart card chip, with a certain amount of storage space, capable of storing the user's private key and digital certificate.
A0025-004.description: Authentication information required for client login (such as username, password, QQ, email, phone, ID number, etc.) can all be written into the USB key. Algorithms and code can also be written in, allowing the key to replace the traditional 'username + password' login method, achieving the goal of only being able to log in to a website or application system when the key is plugged in. Developers can also set the USB key to work alongside the traditional 'username + password' login mode as needed. The USB key can be used for access control, setting different clients to have different permissions — for example, some clients can only use part of the website or system's features, or different clients use different modules. It can also be configured to require the USB key to remain plugged in during use, or to automatically log out after a set time following removal.
A0025-004.limitation: The device is easy to lose or be stolen, potentially leading to unauthorized access to sensitive information. Depends on the login system's support — if the system does not support USB Key login, the USB Key cannot be used.

references.title: FIDO2: Moving the World Beyond Passwords
